nodes.label: Mendeleev's Periodic Table
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Dmitri Mendeleev (Russian chemist) arranged 63 known elements by increasing atomic mass and chemical properties (oxide and hydride formulae). His Periodic Law: properties are periodic function of atomic masses. Achievements: predicted undiscovered elements (Eka-boron=Scandium, Eka-aluminium=Gallium, Eka-silicon=Germanium). Accommodated noble gases later. Limitations: no fixed position for hydrogen, could not explain isotopes, irregular atomic mass sequence (Co before Ni).

nodes.label: Periodic Trends
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Atomic radius: decreases across a period (increasing nuclear charge pulls electrons closer), increases down a group (new shells added). Metallic character: decreases across a period (harder to lose electrons), increases down a group (easier to lose electrons). Electronegativity: increases across a period, decreases down a group. Valency: determined by valence electrons, varies across period but remains same down a group.

nodes.label: Newlands' Law of Octaves
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: John Newlands (1866) arranged elements by increasing atomic mass and found every eighth element had properties similar to the first, like musical octaves. Worked only up to calcium. Limitations: assumed only 56 elements existed, forced unlike elements into same column (e.g., cobalt and nickel with halogens), became irrelevant after discovery of noble gases.

nodes.label: Metalloids (Semi-metals)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Elements at the boundary between metals and non-metals in the periodic table, showing properties of both. The zig-zag line in the Modern Periodic Table separates metals from non-metals. Borderline elements: boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, tellurium, and polonium. Silicon is classified as a metalloid -- used extensively in semiconductor industry. Metals tend to lose electrons (electropositive), non-metals tend to gain (electronegative).

nodes.label: Linkage and Recombination
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Morgan's work on Drosophila showed that genes on the same chromosome do not assort independently (contradicting Mendel's law). Linked genes show parental combinations in higher proportion. Linkage strength is inversely proportional to distance between genes. Recombination frequency used by Sturtevant to map gene positions on chromosomes. Tightly linked genes (e.g., white and yellow in Drosophila, 1.3% recombination) vs loosely linked (e.g., white and miniature wing, 37.2% recombination). Genetic maps used as starting point in genome sequencing projects.

nodes.label: Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Proposed by Sutton and Boveri (1902) after chromosomal behaviour during meiosis was observed to parallel Mendelian gene behaviour. Key parallels: both chromosomes and genes occur in pairs, both segregate at gamete formation, independent pairs segregate independently. Experimentally verified by Thomas Hunt Morgan using Drosophila melanogaster. Genes located on chromosomes; alleles on homologous chromosomes at homologous sites.

nodes.label: Mutation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Alteration in DNA sequences causing changes in genotype and phenotype. Point mutation: change in a single base pair (e.g., sickle-cell anaemia - glutamic acid to valine substitution at 6th position of beta-globin chain due to GAG to GUG codon change). Chromosomal aberrations: loss (deletion) or gain (insertion/duplication) of DNA segments, commonly observed in cancer cells. Frame-shift mutations: insertion or deletion of bases changes reading frame. Mutagens include UV radiation, chemicals.

nodes.label: Down's Syndrome
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Chromosomal disorder caused by trisomy of chromosome 21 (3 copies instead of 2), giving 47 chromosomes total. First described by Langdon Down in 1866. Characteristics: short stature, small round head, furrowed tongue, partially open mouth, broad palm with characteristic palm crease. Physical, psychomotor, and mental development is retarded. Caused by failure of chromosome segregation (non-disjunction) during cell division.

nodes.label: Turner's Syndrome
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Chromosomal disorder caused by monosomy of X chromosome (45, XO karyotype). Affected females have only 45 chromosomes instead of 46. Characteristics: short stature, sterility (rudimentary ovaries), lack of secondary sexual characters. Caused by loss of one X chromosome during cell division. Only affects females.

nodes.label: Klinefelter's Syndrome
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Chromosomal disorder caused by presence of an additional X chromosome in males, giving karyotype 47, XXY. Affected individuals have overall masculine development but also show feminine characteristics like gynaecomastia (breast development). Individuals are sterile. Results from non-disjunction of sex chromosomes.

nodes.label: DNA Structure (Double Helix)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Watson and Crick (1953) proposed the double helix model based on X-ray diffraction data from Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin, and Chargaff's rules (A=T, G=C). Two anti-parallel polynucleotide chains with sugar-phosphate backbone. Base pairing: Adenine-Thymine (2 H-bonds), Guanine-Cytosine (3 H-bonds). Pitch of helix is 3.4 nm with ~10 bp per turn; distance between bp is 0.34 nm. Right-handed coiling. DNA first identified by Friedrich Meischer (1869) as 'Nuclein'. Human haploid genome: 3.3 x 10^9 bp.

nodes.label: DNA Packaging (Chromatin Structure)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: In prokaryotes, DNA is held by proteins in nucleoid region as large loops. In eukaryotes, negatively charged DNA wraps around positively charged histone octamer (rich in lysine and arginine) to form nucleosome (~200 bp each). Nucleosomes form 'beads-on-string' structure visible under electron microscope. Chromatin fibres further coil to form chromosomes at metaphase. Euchromatin: loosely packed, transcriptionally active, stains light. Heterochromatin: densely packed, inactive, stains dark. Total DNA length in a mammalian cell ~2.2 metres.

nodes.label: Metals
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Elements that are generally hard, lustrous, malleable, ductile, sonorous, and good conductors of heat and electricity. Examples include iron, copper, aluminium, calcium, and magnesium. Exceptions exist: sodium and potassium are soft, mercury is liquid at room temperature.

nodes.label: Hardness and Softness
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Materials that are difficult to compress or scratch are called hard (e.g., iron, stone). Materials that can be easily compressed or scratched are called soft (e.g., cotton, sponge). Hardness is an important property for selecting construction and tool materials.

nodes.label: Opaque Materials
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Materials through which objects cannot be seen at all are called opaque. Wood, cardboard, and metals are examples. They block the passage of light completely.

nodes.label: Translucent Materials
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Materials through which objects can be seen but not clearly are called translucent. Oiled paper and frosted glass are examples. They allow partial passage of light.

nodes.label: Rusting of Iron
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Iron reacts with oxygen and moisture in the air to form iron oxide (rust), a reddish-brown substance. Rusting weakens the iron. Prevention methods include painting, oiling, greasing, galvanizing (zinc coating), and chromium plating. Rusting requires both air and moisture.

nodes.label: Stainless Steel
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: An alloy of iron mixed with carbon, chromium, and nickel that resists rusting. The chromium forms a protective oxide layer. Used for making utensils, surgical instruments, and building materials. A practical solution to the rusting problem.

nodes.label: Fungi
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Microorganisms that can be unicellular (yeast) or multicellular (bread mould). Useful in fermentation, bread-making, and antibiotic production (penicillin from Penicillium). Some fungi cause plant diseases like rust of wheat and spoil food under moist conditions.

nodes.label: Communicable Diseases
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Microbial diseases that spread from an infected person to a healthy person through air, water, food, or physical contact. Examples include cholera, common cold, chicken pox, tuberculosis, malaria (via mosquito vector), and dengue. Prevention involves hygiene, vaccination, and vector control.

nodes.label: Lactobacillus
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A beneficial bacterium that converts milk into curd by multiplying in warm milk and promoting curd formation. It is also involved in making cheese, pickles, and other fermented food items. Essential for the preparation of idli and dosa batter along with yeast.

nodes.label: Non-Metals
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Elements that are generally soft, dull, non-malleable, non-ductile, not sonorous, and poor conductors of heat and electricity. Examples include sulphur, carbon, oxygen, and phosphorus. Phosphorus is so reactive it is stored in water to prevent contact with atmospheric oxygen.

nodes.label: Malleability
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The property of metals by which they can be beaten into thin sheets. Silver and aluminium foils are common examples. This characteristic property distinguishes metals from non-metals like coal and sulphur, which break into powder when hammered.

nodes.label: Ductility
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The property of metals by which they can be drawn into wires. Copper and aluminium wires used in electrical circuits demonstrate this property. Non-metals like coal cannot be drawn into wires.

nodes.label: Metallic Oxides
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Oxides formed when metals react with oxygen, which are basic in nature. Iron oxide (rust) and magnesium oxide are examples. Rust is formed when iron reacts with oxygen and water. Copper develops a green coating of copper hydroxide and copper carbonate in moist air.

nodes.label: Non-Metallic Oxides
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Oxides formed when non-metals react with oxygen, which are acidic in nature. Sulphur dioxide dissolved in water forms sulphurous acid, which turns blue litmus paper red. This contrasts with metallic oxides which are basic.

nodes.label: Displacement Reaction
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A chemical reaction where a more reactive metal replaces a less reactive metal from its compound in aqueous solution. Zinc displaces copper from copper sulphate, and iron also displaces copper. The reactivity series determines which metal can displace another.

nodes.label: Element
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A substance that cannot be broken down further by chemical reactions, cooling, heating, or electrolysis. The smallest unit is an atom. There are no more than 94 naturally occurring elements. Most elements are metals, the rest are non-metals or metalloids which possess character of both.

nodes.label: Sonorous Property
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The property of metals to produce a ringing sound when struck hard. This distinguishes metals from non-metals. Church bells and cymbals utilise this property. Wooden or non-metallic objects do not produce such ringing sounds.

nodes.label: Electrical and Thermal Conductivity
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Metals are generally good conductors of both heat and electricity, which is why copper and aluminium are used for electrical wires, and metals are used for cooking utensils. Non-metals are poor conductors, which is why plastic covers electrical wires and wooden handles protect from heat.

nodes.label: Coal
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A hard, black fossil fuel formed about 300 million years ago from dense forests buried under soil. The slow conversion of dead vegetation into coal under high pressure and temperature is called carbonisation. Used in thermal power plants for electricity, in industries, and formerly in railway engines.

nodes.label: Coke
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A tough, porous, black substance that is an almost pure form of carbon, obtained by processing coal. Used in the manufacture of steel and in the extraction of many metals. It is one of the three useful products derived from coal processing.

nodes.label: Coal Tar
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A black, thick liquid with unpleasant smell, a mixture of about 200 substances obtained from coal processing. Products from coal tar serve as starting materials for manufacturing synthetic dyes, drugs, explosives, perfumes, plastics, paints, and naphthalene balls. Now replaced by bitumen for road surfacing.

nodes.label: Petroleum
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A dark oily liquid fossil fuel formed from marine organisms over millions of years, mined from between rocks under the Earth. Called 'black gold' for its commercial importance. In India, found in Assam, Gujarat, Mumbai High, and river basins of Godavari and Krishna. World's first oil well was drilled in Pennsylvania, USA in 1859.

nodes.label: Petroleum Refining
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The process of separating various constituents of petroleum into useful fractions. Products include LPG (home/industry fuel), petrol (motor fuel), kerosene (stoves/jet aircraft), diesel (heavy vehicles), lubricating oil, paraffin wax (candles/ointments), and bitumen (road surfacing/paints).

nodes.label: Carbonisation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The slow process of conversion of dead vegetation into coal over millions of years under high pressure and high temperature conditions. Since coal contains mainly carbon, this process is named carbonisation. It cannot be replicated in the laboratory.

nodes.label: Petrochemicals
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Useful substances obtained from petroleum and natural gas, used for manufacturing detergents, synthetic fibres (polyester, nylon, acrylic), polythene, plastics, and fertilisers (urea from hydrogen gas). They form the backbone of modern chemical industry.

nodes.label: Forest Conservation Act
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: An Indian law aimed at preservation and conservation of natural forests and meeting basic needs of people living in or near forests. It provides the legal framework for protecting forest areas and regulating activities within them.

nodes.label: Metamorphosis
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The transformation of the larva into an adult through drastic changes in body form. In frogs: egg to tadpole to adult frog. In silkworms: egg to caterpillar (larva) to pupa to adult moth. The young forms look very different from the adults.

nodes.label: Pure Substance
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A substance consisting of a single type of particles with the same chemical nature. Has fixed composition and characteristic properties regardless of source. Includes elements (containing one kind of atom) and compounds (formed by chemical combination of elements in fixed ratios).

nodes.label: Distillation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A separation technique used to separate a mixture of two or more miscible liquids with different boiling points. The liquid with lower boiling point vaporises first, is cooled and collected separately. Fractional distillation separates components with close boiling points, used in petroleum refining.

nodes.label: Compound
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A pure substance formed by chemical combination of two or more elements in a fixed ratio. Properties differ from constituent elements. Water (H2O) has properties different from hydrogen and oxygen. Can only be separated into elements by chemical methods, not physical.

nodes.label: Alloy
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A homogeneous mixture (solid solution) of two or more metals, or a metal and a non-metal. Examples include brass (copper + zinc), bronze (copper + tin), and stainless steel (iron + chromium + nickel + carbon). Alloys are classified as mixtures, not compounds.

nodes.label: Subatomic Particles
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Particles smaller than the atom, including electrons (negative charge, discovered by J.J. Thomson, 1897), protons (positive charge, discovered by Goldstein via canal rays), and neutrons (no charge, discovered by Chadwick, 1932). Their discovery disproved Dalton's idea of indivisible atoms.

nodes.label: Electron
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A negatively charged subatomic particle with mass approximately 1/2000th of a hydrogen atom (9.1 x 10^-31 kg). Discovered by J.J. Thomson in 1897 through cathode ray experiments. Electrons revolve around the nucleus in defined orbits or shells.

nodes.label: Proton
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A positively charged subatomic particle found in the nucleus of an atom with mass of about 1 u (1.67 x 10^-27 kg). The number of protons equals the atomic number (Z) and defines the element. Hydrogen has 1 proton, carbon has 6, and oxygen has 8.

nodes.label: Thomson's Model of Atom
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: J.J. Thomson (1906 Nobel Prize) proposed that an atom is a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it, like seeds in a watermelon or currants in a Christmas pudding. Explained electrical neutrality but could not explain Rutherford's scattering results.

nodes.label: Rutherford's Nuclear Model
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Based on the alpha-particle gold foil scattering experiment: most of the atom is empty space, positive charge and mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus (radius 10^5 times less than atom), and electrons revolve around the nucleus. Could not explain why electrons do not spiral into the nucleus.

nodes.label: Bohr's Model of Atom
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Niels Bohr proposed that electrons revolve in discrete circular orbits (shells) around the nucleus without radiating energy. Each orbit has a fixed energy level. Electrons can jump between orbits by absorbing or emitting energy. Shells are designated K, L, M, N with maximum capacities of 2, 8, 18, 32.

nodes.label: Atomic Number
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom, denoted by Z. It determines the identity of the element. In a neutral atom, atomic number equals the number of electrons. Hydrogen Z=1, Carbon Z=6, Oxygen Z=8, Sodium Z=11.

nodes.label: Mass Number
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom, denoted by A. Mass number = Atomic number + Number of neutrons. For example, carbon-12 has A=12 (6 protons + 6 neutrons) while carbon-14 has A=14 (6 protons + 8 neutrons).

nodes.label: Isotopes
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers due to different numbers of neutrons. Examples: hydrogen (protium, deuterium, tritium), carbon-12 and carbon-14, chlorine-35 and chlorine-37. Used in medicine (cobalt-60 for cancer), nuclear energy (uranium-235), and carbon dating.

nodes.label: Isobars
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Atoms of different elements having the same mass number but different atomic numbers. For example, calcium-40 (Z=20) and argon-40 (Z=18) are isobars as both have mass number 40 but are different elements with different chemical properties.

nodes.label: Electronic Configuration
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The distribution of electrons in various shells/orbits of an atom following the formula 2n^2 for maximum electrons per shell (K=2, L=8, M=18). The outermost shell cannot have more than 8 electrons. The number of electrons in the outermost shell determines an element's chemical properties and valency.

nodes.label: J.J. Thomson
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: British physicist (1856-1940) who discovered the electron in 1897 and proposed the first atomic model. Awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1906. Directed the Cavendish Laboratory at Cambridge for 35 years; seven of his research assistants subsequently won Nobel prizes.

nodes.label: Golgi Apparatus
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Discovered by Camillo Golgi (1906 Nobel Prize), it consists of membrane-bound vesicles (cisternae) stacked parallel. Functions include packaging and dispatching cell products, making lysosomes, and modifying proteins/lipids made in the ER for transport.

nodes.label: Principle of Vaccination
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Based on the immune system's ability to remember pathogens. Introducing weakened or killed microbes trains the immune system to fight the actual pathogen quickly when encountered. Provides long-lasting protection. Smallpox was eradicated globally through mass vaccination programmes.

nodes.label: Principles of Disease Prevention
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Two approaches: general (public health measures like clean water, sanitation, nutrition, hygiene, avoiding crowding) and specific (vaccination against particular diseases). Prevention is better than cure because treatment only works after damage has started.
